messages.body_plain:
Thanks for these details!  I definitely agree with you that part of
the issue is the fact that there are so many absolute 0 proportions in
the data.

That said, I still think these results are providing better
information, and I think if anything it's just a reminder that
z/t-values and p-values are not effect sizes!  I think what's
bothering you is that the p-value is so small for the cond1 - cond2
effect, but then the effect for cond1 - cond3 is SO much larger, and
consistently very large, but "less reliable."  To put it another way:
looking subject-by-subject, there is a nice consistent effect of cond2
> cond1 for every person, ranging from about .05 to about .20.  But
then looking at the differences between cond1 and cond3, there is a
consistent, huge effect, no less than .57, most in the .70-.90 range.
How could this possibly be less reliable than the cond 2 > cond1
effect?

Here's how I understand it (which of course could be mistaken!). If
you think about effect sizes, the model results match what your eyes
are telling you. With an effect of -20.8 and a std err of 8.7, this
puts the "top" of the 95% confidence interval around an effect of
-3.75 or so. In other words, you can be pretty sure that the effect
expected from the population is at least -3.75 log-odds, which is a
pretty darn big effect!  But with a confidence interval from -3.75 to
about -37.8, that's a lot of uncertainty in the actual size of the
effect.  That uncertainty is coming from the fact that you only have
two people that have any positive responses at all. The one person
with 6% positive responses has an effect of around -4.75 logit.
That's a lot less negative than the overall estimate!  So that's where
the large variance estimate for the random slope is coming from, and
why there is a lot of uncertainty around the effect of condition 3.
But you can also see that even with all this uncertainty, the model
tells you to expect the cond1 - cond 3 difference to be much larger
(in logit terms) than the cond1 - cond2 difference, which is exactly
what you see when eye-balling the data. The fact that there's more
uncertainty in one effect doesn't mean the expected effect size is
smaller.

So if you walk through the confidence intervals, basically the random
intercept model is saying that you expect the positive response rate
in condition 3 to be around 1%, maybe as high as 3%, whereas the
random slope model is telling you that you should expect a response
rate virtually at zero, but maybe as high as 9%.  Given that your
actual subjects varied from 0% to 6%, it seems to me that the random
slope model is providing more accurate predictive estimates to what
you might expect to see if you grabbed 10 more random subjects and
expected to see a similar pattern.

But you might also point out that there are a few people with 100%
positive responses in condition 2.  A logit of 1 is Inf (just like a
logit of 0 is -Inf), so why is the variance estimate so much smaller
for condition 2 than for condition 3?  Since the effect between
anything and 100% is a difference of infinite logits, shouldn't that
also make the variance in condition 2 huge? I think the answer has to
do with the fact that only 3 out of 10 people have 100% in condition
2, where it's 8 of 10 people with 0% in condition 3. The way random
effects are estimated results in "shrinkage" of each subject's random
effects towards a more central value. The result is that the estimate
is pulled much lower (more negative) for condition 3, since "central"
IS quite extreme because there are many extreme low values, where
there are only a few extreme high values in condition 2.

Again, I think a careful addition of some "noise" so that you have
fewer people responding at 0% is really the way to go here.  The
simplest, but maybe impractical, strategy would be to add enough items
so that people were likely to get one or two responses of "1" (even if
they actually meant to respond "0"), to the point that at least most
of your subjects were not at 0% or 100%.  A strategy that would
require a lot more care and thought (and maybe some simulation
studies) would be to add some noise artificially to your data.

So to recap my argument here: if your conclusion is that the random
slope model is incoherent or obviously "wrong", I disagree. I still
think the random slope model is giving you a better description of
your data than the random intercept model, more consistent with the
prediction that if you grabbed more people, you'd expect most people
to be at 0% in condition 3, but maybe a couple of people in the 3-9%
range. If your prediction followed the random intercept model, you'd
be much more surprised to see another person hit around 6% in
condition 3 (i.e., you'd be very surprised to see the same pattern of
data that you've already collected). If your conclusion is that these
models provide really extreme (and uncertain) estimates when you have
a design that results in most subjects performing at 0% or 100%, I
absolutely agree.  If this is a frequent occurrence for you, I think
it would be worth it to explore other types of modeling (Bayesian, or
maybe non-linear or non-parametric models), or explore techniques for
carefully transforming your data (like adding a little noise), or
consider making more items so that you get fewer 0%/100% rates from
individuals.

my two cents,

So yes, I think the common issue here is that when one of the possible binary responses is extremely rare, resulting in many people/items that show completely uniform responses in that cell, then estimating the random slopes for those people is going to be pretty tough.
>
> However, I'm not sure that it means that fitting the random intercept-only model is "better," necessarily. I think it can be helpful to think about what the estimates are telling you here.

> (by the way, I don't think you have your log-odds formula right:)

> logit <- function(p) log(p/(1-p))
>
> So logit(.79) = 1.32, and logit(.009) = -4.70
>
> And if you look at the estimate for your intercept-only model, the difference between conditions 1 and 3 is around -6 log-odds.  In other words, that model is giving you basically the same results as if you had completely ignored the fact that these data are repeated-measures data, and just looked at the log-odds difference between 1 and 3 (1.32
> - -4.70 = about 6, same as the model estimate).
>
> But of course, it *is* repeated measures data!  And the model that tries to take that into account is giving you a MUCH larger (negative) estimate for the difference between 1 and 3.  A log-odds of -19.4 (1.4
> + -20.8) is really really close to zero (i.e., a 4 with 8 zeros in
> front of it).  So in my mind, the model is basically telling you that if you wanted to guess the most likely results of some new subjects, you'd be most accurate if you were to guess that they would have all zeros in that cell.  But it's also telling you that maybe subjects vary a lot, so maybe you'd get a weirdo who would respond differently.
>  In other words, it's an enormous effect, but maybe not so reliable across people.
>
> And now I'm noticing that there are only 10 people in your data.
> Definitely not too many to plot individually!  I'd guess that if you plot them individually, you'd see something like 9 of them with all zeros, and one person with like 3 responses of 1.  I'm guessing about the data here, but with 1022 observations and ten people, you basically have roughly 30+ responses in each condition per person.
> The overall .009 proportion in condition 3 means about 3 or so responses of "1" total in the entire data set in that condition.  If all three of those "1" responses are coming from a single subject, then that one person would have something like 10% (or log-odds -2.2) for condition 3, which would be less than half the effect size of -6 predicted by the intercept-only model. In intuitive terms, the -6 effect size would be just not as reliable as the intercept-only model is telling you, since 1 out of 10 people show a much smaller effect (and 9 out of 10 are showing a much much larger effect!).
>
> Of course, I'm just guessing on whether your data actually looks like this.  But if I'm right about what the subject-by-subject data are, then the random slopes model is actually telling you the "right"
> answer: namely that you basically expect all zeros (or close to it) in that condition, but there may be people who have significantly more 1s, to the point where the effect may not be quite as reliable as you'd hope for, across a random sample of new people.
>
> But yes, this kind of thing is really exaggerated when you have completely uniform responses from a number of people (i.e., 0% or 100%), because those logit estimates are going to tend towards infinity.  It would be good to have some simulations or other research on the best practices when the data are this skewed, but in the meantime, I think the results the models are giving you actually seem reasonable, given what I'm imagining your data looks like.
>
> Two possible more practical things to try when you are collecting data that is so close to 0% or 100% are (1) to make sure you collect a lot more data, so that you're at least getting *some* responses of both types from most of your subjects (even if that's just a little noise), or (2) artificially add a little "noise" yourself, by adding a couple of 1s to everyone's data.  You'd have to think through the latter a lot more (how many to add, how random to make it, how to distribute the 1s across conditions, etc.), but it might help get you away from the boundary of 0% enough to get what appear to be more stable estimates.
